origin: Original workshop built by Muse (AI assistant) on 19 November 2026 at Steven Powell's direction, from his pick in the Everyday Cool ideas side chat that evening: of four queued STEM rooms (Math, Engineering, Earth, Computing — a list he ordered saved so all four will be built), he chose Engineering first, in his words: 'lets do Engieering. That links to/from survival too.' The room teaches the six simple machines (lever, wheel & axle, pulley, inclined plane, wedge, and the screw stated exactly as a ramp wrapped around a pole), each with everyday anchors, and carries four playable benches with the working shown: a lever bench (fulcrum slider; MA = effort arm / load arm; a 90 kg crate at 0.5 m on a 3 m beam lifts with 18 kg of push), a pulley bench (1-4 rope segments; effort = load / segments, rope pulled = segments x lift, friction named), a ramp bench (effort = load x sin(slope), read for a 1 m climb against the 1:12 wheelchair-ramp standard, about 4.8 degrees, ADA section 405.2), and a frames bench (a pushed square racks by the full push; a triangle and a braced square lean zero). Wedge and screw cards carry inline SVG diagrams; a rules section states that mechanical advantage multiplies force, never energy, and carries the rigging safety lines. The Survival Guide cross-link runs both ways, as Steven specified: this room's 'Out in the field' section links to the Guide, and the Guide's Links Out section gained a 'machine shop' card linking back. The banner is AI-generated watercolor: the plush robot in a yellow engineer's hard hat holding a rolled blueprint, beside a lever beam on a stone fulcrum and a pulley hoisting a crate, chalk lever/pulley/triangle diagrams behind — no readable lettering, shipped on its first generation. It enters the catalog under 'Science' with hubParent 'stem-room', immediately after Everyday Measure, as the twenty-sixth entry and the STEM Room's seventh workshop. This folder is the maintained original. Folded into the same build at Steven's mid-flight instruction: a pocket log table section (ninety four-decimal mantissas for 1.0-9.9, characteristic-plus-mantissa lookups with linear interpolation — proportional parts — and a worked example, log 2.53; the bench computes by the table's rounded values on purpose, wobble visible; the slide rule named as the table turned into lengths). No forward link to the not-yet-built Everyday Math room; the pending cross-link is recorded in the room's COLLECTION.md for the Math build to close both ways.
